background: Online monotone subsequence selection is a clean sequential-selection problem at the boundary of applied probability, optimal stopping, and online algorithms. A sequence of iid continuous observations arrives one at a time, and the decision maker must irrevocably select an increasing subsequence. The offline longest increasing subsequence has famous $2\sqrt n$ first-order behavior; the online constrained version has first-order constant $\sqrt{2}$. The first-order law is classical. The later second-order analysis resolves the bounded-versus-divergent question formerly posed here.
full_statement: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. observations from a continuous distribution, reduced to uniform observations on $[0,1]$ by the probability integral transform. An online nonanticipating policy irrevocably accepts an increasing subsequence. Write $v_n=\sup_\pi\mathbb E[L_n^\pi]$ for its optimal expected length and $g(n)=\sqrt{2n}-v_n$. The historical question asked whether $g(n)$ is bounded or diverges and, if it diverges, at what rate. Seksenbayev (2021), Theorem 1, answers it: $$v_n=\sqrt{2n}-\frac{1}{12}\log n+O(1),\qquad g(n)=\frac{1}{12}\log n+O(1).$$ This is a fixed-sample-size result, not just a Poissonized approximation.
open_problem: Resolved: the deficit has logarithmic growth with coefficient $1/12$.
known_results: Samuels and Steele established the first-order scale; Arlotto, Wei, and Xie gave an adaptive policy with logarithmic additive guarantees. Seksenbayev, Acta Applicandae Mathematicae 174, article 6 (2021), Theorem 1, proves the expansion in full_statement directly for fixed $n$. Section 2.2 compares trial functions with the discrete Bellman recursion and bounds the remainder. Section 2.3 also proves an $O(1)$ gap for the adaptive square-root-window policy. These results settle this record's stated target, without identifying a limit for the bounded remainder.

where_posed.text: Posed in the concluding discussion of Arlotto, Wei, and Xie, 'An adaptive O(log n)-optimal policy for the online selection of a monotone subsequence from a random sample'.

progress.summary: Theorem 1 identifies the logarithmic deficit and its coefficient, with bounded error.

counterexample_rationale: The asymptotic deficit question is resolved analytically; finite examples cannot overturn that theorem.
alphaevolve_rationale: Computation may examine the bounded remainder or illustrate the published asymptotic law, not rediscover the resolved logarithmic term.

literature.synthesis: First-order asymptotics and logarithmic-gap policies were followed by a direct Bellman comparison establishing the second-order expansion. Thus boundedness of the original deficit is no longer an open alternative. A sharper analysis of the bounded remainder would be a different question.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Verify the discrete Bellman comparison in Seksenbayev, Section 2.2, before proposing any finer-order extension.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: Use the optimal value v_n, not one policy's value. Check the fixed-n theorem rather than transferring a Poissonized expansion without an error bound.

notes_for_maintainer: Audit 2026-11-09: the 2021 published theorem resolves the exact question. Full-text model, Theorem 1, its comparison argument, and Section 2.3 read. Do not silently replace the record by an unverified higher-order open problem.
short_statement: The optimal online expected length is $v_n=\sqrt{2n}-(1/12)\log n+O(1)$; the second-order deficit is logarithmic (Seksenbayev, 2021).
